blocks.text: Most Jack Ma stories jump from a rejected job application straight to a Hangzhou apartment. The real list is longer and much messier. Before Alibaba he ran a translation shop that lost money for three years, a web company he lost to a state telecom, and a government internet project he walked out of. He has counted all three as failures himself.

Below is every company, fund and major project we could verify, in the order they began. Some are giants. Some were dead within two years. For each one we show the idea, the decision, the first money and what really happened. __Read the small failures closely, because almost every later win reuses a lesson from one of them.__
Start with the flops. They paid for everything after.
Before Alibaba: three false starts

blocks.name: Hope Translation Agency (Haibo)
blocks.idea: Ma was a young college English lecturer who was getting known for his language skills. Businesses needed translators, and there was no professional translation shop in Hangzhou. So he opened one with colleagues and named it Hope.
blocks.decision: China's business climate was warming in 1992 and he wanted to do more than teach, but he had been turned down for job after job. The key decision came later. Selling gifts was earning several thousand yuan a month while translation earned a few hundred, and colleagues told him to drop translation and become a gift shop. He refused, because translation was the reason the shop existed.
blocks.howStarted: A room of about 30 square metres in Hangzhou and five staff. He kept his teaching job at the same time.
blocks.funding: He and colleagues pooled 3,000 yuan. Rent alone was reported at 1,500 to 2,000 yuan a month, and the first month's income was under 1,000 yuan.
blocks.whatHappened: To cover the rent he took trains to Yiwu carrying large sacks, bought flowers and small gifts wholesale, and resold them. He split the office in half, one side translation and one side gifts. He also spent over a year selling medicine and medical equipment to hospitals and clinics. A cashier was caught skimming 100 to 200 yuan a day for months before anyone noticed. The agency finally turned a profit in 1995 after three years of losses, and press reports in 2014 called it the largest in Hangzhou.
blocks.lesson: Do not wait until you are big to set up money controls. And side income is fine if it keeps your real business alive, as long as you remember which one is the real business.

blocks.name: China Pages
blocks.idea: A company that built and hosted web pages for Chinese businesses, so foreign buyers could find them. It came from one search in Seattle in 1995. Ma typed beer into Yahoo and found nothing from China.
blocks.decision: A simple page for his translation shop drew five emails from abroad within a day, and that convinced him. Back home he pitched two dozen friends and 23 of them told him not to do it. He quit teaching anyway. The second big decision came when China Telecom launched a rival service. He could fight a state giant or take its money, and he took the money.
blocks.howStarted: Ma and a few others, in Hangzhou, in April 1995. He had never used a keyboard before that trip and later compared himself to a blind rider on a blind tiger. To prove the internet was real he invited friends and TV people home and waited three and a half hours on dial-up for half a page to load.
blocks.funding: About $2,000 borrowed from friends and family. Chinese reports describe the same money as about 20,000 yuan.
blocks.whatHappened: The site reportedly earned about 5 million yuan in under three years, making it one of China's earliest internet businesses. After roughly a year of competing, China Telecom put in the equivalent of $185,000 by Ma's account, or $240,000 for 70% by Forbes's. The telecom side got five board seats and Ma got two. A board is the small group that votes on a company's big decisions, so he was outvoted every time. He called it an elephant against an ant, and he resigned.
blocks.lesson: Read the control terms before you read the cheque. Board seats, not money, decide who really runs a company.

blocks.name: Guofutong, the foreign trade ministry's e-commerce unit
blocks.idea: Build websites for China's Ministry of Foreign Trade, including an online market for Chinese goods. It was a state-backed try at the idea Ma already believed in.
blocks.decision: After leaving China Pages he accepted an invitation to Beijing to run this unit. The fight that ended it was about customers. The ministry wanted to serve big state companies, while Ma wanted to serve small firms. One night in 1998 he gathered his team in his room and told them where he stood. He left in January 1999.
blocks.howStarted: He moved north with people from Hangzhou. Reports of the group's size differ, from 5 to 12, but the names listed include Eddie Wu, Peng Lei and Sun Tongyu, who all later became senior Alibaba leaders. One report says they shared a rented room of about 20 square metres.
blocks.funding: Government money. China Securities Journal reported 2 million yuan of start-up funding and a promise of a 30% stake for the team.
blocks.whatHappened: The same report says the team earned 2.87 million yuan in net profit in 15 months while living on a few thousand yuan a month, and that the promised stake was hard to pin down inside the state system. The sites did well, but Ma had no ownership and no freedom. The job did give him something valuable: it was how he met Yahoo co-founder Jerry Yang in 1998. The unit outlived his time there.
blocks.lesson: If your stake is not in writing, you do not have one. But a bad deal can still be a good school, if you leave with the contacts and the team.

blocks.text: The team followed him out. That team became Alibaba.
The core: what the fortune was built on

blocks.name: Alibaba.com (business-to-business marketplace)
blocks.idea: A website where small Chinese exporters could list products and be found by overseas buyers. Business-to-business, or B2B, means companies selling to companies rather than to shoppers.
blocks.decision: He picked small firms on purpose, because that was the argument he had just lost in Beijing. He has said the model was designed in-house, not copied from an American site. He picked the name because people everywhere know the Ali Baba tale and its magic door to treasure, and it was easy to spell.
blocks.howStarted: Ma's apartment in the Lakeside Gardens estate in Hangzhou, with 18 people listening to him talk for two hours. The site went live in March 1999, and the holding company's legal founding date is 28 June 1999. Joe Tsai, a Yale-trained lawyer at the investment firm Investor AB, met Ma that May and joined for $50 a month.
blocks.funding: About $60,000 put on the table by the 18 founders. Next came $5 million in October 1999, with Goldman Sachs putting in $3.3 million of it, then a $20 million round led by SoftBank in January 2000.
blocks.whatHappened: By July 2000 it had close to 200,000 members but revenue of perhaps $1 million, and Forbes put its value at no more than $50 million. It nearly ran out of cash in 2001. A paid product for exporters saved it, and by the end of 2002 it made a profit of one dollar. It listed in Hong Kong in 2007 and was taken private in 2012. By 2020 this original business was under 3% of the group's value, yet its cash had funded Taobao and Alipay.
blocks.lesson: Your first product does not need to be your biggest. It needs to throw off enough cash and trust to pay for the next one.

blocks.name: Alibaba's first global expansion
blocks.idea: Become a world company immediately, with offices in Silicon Valley, Hong Kong, Europe and South Korea. At a staff party in 2000 Ma was promising a top-ten global website.
blocks.decision: Ma later said the Silicon Valley plan came from a smart American MBA and sounded right. It took only about a month and a half to see the flaw: the trade experts they needed had to be flown in from New York and San Francisco to work among engineers, and costs kept climbing.
blocks.howStarted: Hiring raced ahead of revenue after the 2000 funding. The US office grew to about 40 people. Hong Kong had about 30.
blocks.funding: The $25 million raised from Goldman Sachs, SoftBank and others in 1999 and 2000.
blocks.whatHappened: By early 2001 the company was burning about $2 million a month. Nearly the whole US office was let go, Hong Kong fell to 8 people and all South Korea staff were laid off with three months' pay. Total staff fell from about 360 to 150 in 30 days.
blocks.lesson: Having money in the bank is not a reason to open offices. Open one only when customers in that place are already asking for you.

blocks.text: He raised the money, then nearly died of spending it.

blocks.name: Taobao
blocks.idea: A consumer marketplace where anyone could list anything for free. The name means digging for treasure.
blocks.decision: This was defence. eBay bought a third of China's EachNet in 2002 and the rest in 2003. Ma could see that in China a small business owner and a shopper were often the same person, so eBay would eventually reach his customers. He chose to attack first, and to charge nothing.
blocks.howStarted: A secret team worked from Ma's old apartment during the 2003 SARS outbreak. An early insider recalled rolling power cuts and people sleeping on the floor until the electricity came back. It launched in May 2003.
blocks.funding: Inside money, not a new outside company. SoftBank put a series of investments totalling $50 million into the Taobao entity in 2003 and 2004, according to Alibaba's prospectus.
blocks.whatHappened: eBay held over 70% of the market at launch. By the end of 2004 the race was 39% to 37%. Taobao passed eBay by 2006, eBay became the junior partner in a joint venture that December, and by 2008 Taobao held over 80%.
blocks.lesson: When a rival's model depends on fees, free can be a weapon, as long as you have another business paying your bills.

blocks.name: Alipay, later Ant Group
blocks.idea: Few Chinese shoppers had credit cards, and strangers did not trust each other online. Alipay worked as escrow: a neutral party holds the buyer's money and pays the seller only after the goods arrive.
blocks.decision: China had no clear rules for private payment services, so launching it was a legal risk. Ma took the risk himself and told staff he would be the one to go to jail if it came to that. After a heated internal debate, the company also chose to open Alipay to outsiders rather than keep it for Taobao alone.
blocks.howStarted: As an Alibaba unit, set up as a separate company in December 2004 and built around Taobao's trust problem.
blocks.funding: Alibaba's own money first. After it was renamed Ant Financial in October 2014, it raised outside money: a first round in July 2015 at a value of $45 billion, $4.5 billion in 2016 at $60 billion, and about $14 billion in 2018 at about $150 billion.
blocks.whatHappened: It moved out of Alibaba into a company controlled by Ma in 2011, which caused a bitter fight with Yahoo. Its Yu'ebao fund let people save from just one yuan and held 1.7 trillion yuan by March 2018. In 2020 it was days from a record stock listing that regulators stopped. It was restructured, fined $984 million in 2023 and revalued at $78.54 billion. As far as we could find, it had still not listed by late 2026.
blocks.lesson: Solve the trust problem and you own the customer. But once you hold people's money, regulators become your most important audience.

blocks.text: If someone has to go to jail, I'll go.
blocks.who: Jack Ma, to colleagues when Alipay launched

blocks.text: Brave in 2004. Remember this line when you reach 2020.

Alibaba's next few years brought lots of experiments. Several came out of the 2005 Yahoo deal, which handed Alibaba a famous brand it never managed to turn into a business. Others were attempts to make money from the sellers Taobao had attracted for free. __Notice how many of these got folded into something else instead of being announced as failures.__ Big companies rarely hold a funeral.

blocks.name: Yahoo China
blocks.idea: Run Yahoo's Chinese portal and search business. It was part of the deal: Yahoo gave Alibaba $1 billion plus this unit in exchange for about 40% of Alibaba.
blocks.decision: The deal was a package, so taking Yahoo's cash meant taking the portal too. Running a large foreign-branded web portal was nothing like his core business.
blocks.howStarted: Bought rather than built. Staff numbered about 2,000 at the 2006 to 2007 peak, according to a former general manager.
blocks.funding: No new money was spent. It was contributed by Yahoo as part of the 2005 investment.
blocks.whatHappened: Users and market share fell year after year. Analysts blamed weak localisation and the lack of attention from a company focused on its own brands. Music closed in January 2013 and email in August 2013, and news and community services shut that September. Staff had fallen below 100. A former general manager said the purchase achieved nothing.
blocks.lesson: A famous brand does not transfer automatically. If you buy something you have no plan for, it slowly dies on your balance sheet.

blocks.name: Alisoft
blocks.idea: Online business software for China's small companies, covering customer records, stock, sales teams and finances. Under 10% of China's 40 million small firms used such systems.
blocks.decision: The bet was that the same small firms using Alibaba would pay for tools to run their shops. It looked like an obvious extra product.
blocks.howStarted: Launched in January 2007. It offered the software free at first and took over Alibaba's messaging tools, merged under the name Ali Wangwang.
blocks.funding: Funded inside Alibaba Group. No separate amount was disclosed in the sources we could check.
blocks.whatHappened: It did not last as a stand-alone company. In July 2009 it merged into the group's research institute, and that August Alibaba.com bought its business software division for 208 million yuan. Two years, then folded in.
blocks.lesson: A big customer base does not guarantee a second product will sell. Being free for the first months does not prove anyone will pay later.

blocks.name: Koubei
blocks.idea: A local reviews and services site. Think of it as a guide to nearby restaurants and shops, the part of life online stores could not reach.
blocks.decision: Alibaba bought in as a strategic investor in 2006 to reach local spending. Then it kept moving the business around, which is usually a sign nobody knows where it belongs.
blocks.howStarted: Bought into rather than founded. Alibaba invested in the site in 2006.
blocks.funding: The 2006 amount was not found in reliable sources. The 2015 relaunch had 3 billion yuan each from Alibaba and Ant Financial, nearly $1 billion in total.
blocks.whatHappened: It merged with Yahoo China in June 2008 as Yahoo Koubei, then moved into Taobao in August 2009. Six years later the name returned as a joint venture aimed at food and local services, with Alibaba and Ant owning half each.
blocks.lesson: A good name can outlive a bad plan. Before you buy into something, decide who inside your company owns it.

blocks.name: Taobao Mall, later Tmall
blocks.idea: Online stores for proper brands, separate from Taobao's free-for-all. It would solve two problems at once: shoppers worried about fakes, and Taobao still needed a way to earn money.
blocks.decision: When Taobao tried selling top spots by auction, there was a backlash, but about 40% of the market liked the idea because they linked higher-paying sellers with better quality. Alibaba read that as demand for a premium zone. That data point gave Tmall its reason to exist.
blocks.howStarted: Launched in 2008. It was struggling to attract brands. In 2009 its head, Daniel Zhang, wanted people to notice it, so his team ran a sale on 11 November with 27 brands.
blocks.funding: Funded from Alibaba Group and Taobao's budget. No separate outside round was found.
blocks.whatHappened: That first sale brought in 52 million yuan against a normal 8 million a day. By 2013 the day took in 36.2 billion yuan with 254 million orders. Zhang later said he never expected it to become a national event, and he went on to become Alibaba's CEO. In 2011 a steep fee rise sparked a merchant revolt.
blocks.lesson: A marketing stunt for an unknown product can become the product's whole identity. Run small experiments and watch which ones refuse to stop growing.

blocks.text: Singles' Day began as a way to get noticed. Twenty-seven brands.

blocks.name: Alibaba Cloud (Aliyun)
blocks.idea: Build giant shared computing systems from scratch, so Alibaba's own sites would not rely on expensive foreign hardware, and then rent that computing power out to others. Cloud computing means renting computers over the internet instead of buying them.
blocks.decision: Ma pushed the idea at a time when, a Chinese report says, even other internet founders dismissed cloud computing as old wine in a new bottle or centuries away. He brought in Wang Jian, a professor who had headed a psychology department and then worked at Microsoft Research Asia. Wang joined as chief architect in 2008 and insisted on writing the core system in-house instead of using open-source software.
blocks.howStarted: Founded in 2009 inside Alibaba. An early internal customer was Alibaba's small-loans team, whose boss was told by Ma to use the product even though it miscalculated loan amounts at first.
blocks.funding: Alibaba's own profits. The total early budget has not been confirmed by a filing.
blocks.whatHappened: Senior engineers quit and colleagues openly called Wang a liar. He broke down in tears at a 2012 company event. In the internal forum, people mocked his promotion to chief technology officer and Ma personally defended him. In 2013 the system finally ran 5,000 servers as one machine. By the June 2026 quarter this business earned 48.4 billion yuan, up 45% in a year, and had become the centre of Alibaba's AI strategy.
blocks.lesson: Some bets take years to show results and will look stupid the whole time. If you make one, the founder has to personally absorb the criticism.

blocks.name: YunOS / Aliyun OS (phone operating system)
blocks.idea: An Alibaba-owned phone operating system, so shoppers moving from PCs to phones would keep buying through Alibaba and not depend on Google's Android. An executive said the aim was to become China's Android.
blocks.decision: Wang Jian proposed it in 2010 while the cloud project was itself still shaky. Ma later wrote that he was almost angry at the boldness of it. He approved it anyway.
blocks.howStarted: Launched in July 2011 on hardware from young partners. Early phones were reported to crash, black out and frustrate staff who had bought them as gifts for family.
blocks.funding: Alibaba's internal budget. No separate figure was found.
blocks.whatHappened: It reached over one million phones within about a year, by Alibaba's count. On 13 September 2012 journalists arrived in Shanghai for an Acer phone launch and found the doors closed. Alibaba said Google had threatened to end its Android cooperation with Acer. Google said Aliyun was an incompatible version of Android, which Alibaba denied. In 2015 TechCrunch still described it as not having taken off. It never became a real rival to Android.
blocks.lesson: If your product depends on a partner who also depends on your competitor, your competitor holds the off switch.

blocks.text: Ma's own money, and the wider empire

Around 2010 Ma began putting his name on things outside Alibaba. The first was an investment firm. One line in Alibaba's IPO paperwork shows how carefully these side deals could be structured. When Alibaba lent co-founder Simon Xie 6.5 billion yuan to back an investment in the media company Wasu, Ma also took part, but the filing says his financial interest was limited to getting back his own 99,000 yuan.

blocks.name: Yunfeng Capital
blocks.idea: A private equity fund investing in Chinese internet, consumer and new energy companies. Private equity means pooling big investors' money to buy stakes in companies. The name joins the given names of Ma Yun and David Yu Feng.
blocks.decision: Ma co-founded it with David Yu of Target Media and other entrepreneurs, keeping it separate from Alibaba. He later committed to giving all his economic interest in the fund's managing partner to charity, a detail worth noticing.
blocks.howStarted: Established in April 2010 with David Yu as chairman.
blocks.funding: About 10 billion yuan ($1.52 billion) through two funds by January 2011, with a $10 million minimum. Surprisingly, an anchor investor was Tencent, Alibaba's great rival. Fund II raised about $1.1 billion in 2014, with $100 million committed by Alibaba.
blocks.whatHappened: It bought into Sogou alongside Alibaba, and backed deals with Alibaba including Youku Tudou and CITIC 21CN. Its listed arm, Yunfeng Financial, bought 10,000 ether for $44 million in 2025 as a reserve asset, warning investors about how volatile the crypto market is.
blocks.lesson: Once you are successful, your reputation is itself a source of capital. Other founders, even rivals, will invest alongside you.

blocks.name: Laiwang
blocks.idea: A messaging app to stop Tencent's WeChat from taking over Chinese mobile life. A revamped version launched in September 2013, hoping for 30% of the market.
blocks.decision: Alibaba saw WeChat as a threat to its future, as phones became the way people shopped. Ma backed Laiwang personally. Rather than ask whether people wanted another chat app, the company tried to force the numbers.
blocks.howStarted: Built inside Alibaba. A reported internal push required each employee to recruit 100 outside users in a month, and famous business figures were signed up to attract people.
blocks.funding: Alibaba's own money. Chinese business press 36Kr reported a bet of 1 billion yuan, though this figure is not from a filing.
blocks.whatHappened: It never reached critical mass. Critical mass is the point at which a network has enough users that it grows by itself. Friends stay where their friends already are, and they were on WeChat. It stands as one of Ma's clearest product defeats. The one useful thing it produced was research into workplace messaging.
blocks.lesson: You cannot order people to love a product. A social network is the one business where a rival's lead grows stronger every day.

blocks.name: DingTalk
blocks.idea: Workplace chat for small companies, showing bosses and teams who had read a message and whether a task was moving. WeChat was built for friends, and this was built for offices.
blocks.decision: Laiwang's team had noticed the demand while looking for features that could set it apart. Instead of shutting down, the team led by Chen Hang turned to the one thing WeChat did not focus on.
blocks.howStarted: In May 2014 about 20 people moved into Ma's old Lakeside Gardens flat of 150 square metres. They worked on couches and on the balcony on takeaway food. The first version came out about eight months later.
blocks.funding: Alibaba's internal budget.
blocks.whatHappened: By 2018 it had over 100 million users and 7 million employers. Some workers disliked how it let bosses monitor them, and that backlash made news. Alibaba's 2026 results describe its new AI workplace agent as deeply tied into DingTalk.
blocks.lesson: A failed product can leave you with real customer insight. Keep the team and the finding even after you kill the app.

blocks.text: Same team. Same rival. Different question. Different result.

blocks.name: Cainiao (logistics)
blocks.idea: A shared data network tying together China's delivery companies, launched with partner firms, aimed at the delivery bottleneck in online shopping.
blocks.decision: Alibaba chose to link up existing delivery firms rather than own every van. The 2023 plan to spin it off with its own IPO was reversed in 2024, when management said the unit was too strategic to let go and decided to double down.
blocks.howStarted: Founded on 28 May 2013. Its first e-waybill, a digital shipping label, went out in May 2014.
blocks.funding: Alibaba and partner firms. By 2017 Alibaba held 47% and paid 5.3 billion yuan to reach 51%, in a deal that suggested a value near $20 billion. It pledged 100 billion yuan over five years. The founding amounts were not confirmed in filings we could read.
blocks.whatHappened: It was still loss-making in 2017. In March 2024 Alibaba withdrew its Hong Kong listing application and offered minority holders $0.62 a share, up to $3.75 billion, for the rest of the company.
blocks.lesson: You can solve a bottleneck without owning it, if you control the data that everyone else needs.

blocks.name: Alibaba Pictures (formerly ChinaVision)
blocks.idea: Buy into films and media to supply content for Alibaba's TV and video plans, in what looked set to become the world's largest movie market.
blocks.decision: Alibaba moved quickly, buying control of a listed Hong Kong film company just before its own IPO. The speed became the problem.
blocks.howStarted: Bought rather than built. The deal cost about $804 million and completed in 2014.
blocks.funding: Alibaba's cash.
blocks.whatHappened: Less than two months later, the new company reported possible accounting problems and its shares were halted, which raised awkward questions about how well Alibaba had checked the deal. It was still being described as loss-making in 2018, when Variety called its big fantasy film Asura the most expensive flop in Chinese history. Alibaba added about $160 million that year to take majority control.
blocks.lesson: Check the books before you sign, especially when you are in a hurry. Speed is an advantage in product and a danger in acquisitions.

blocks.name: Guangzhou Evergrande football club stake
blocks.idea: Half of China's most successful football club, at a time when Chinese leaders were pushing to develop the sport.
blocks.decision: This is one of the oddest big deals in the book. Reuters described it as hatched over a few drinks, and CNN reported it was finalised in a 15-minute phone call the next day. Ma openly said he did not understand football.
blocks.howStarted: A personal conversation between Ma and the club's owner, property tycoon Xu Jiayin of Evergrande.
blocks.funding: $192 million from Alibaba, for 50%.
blocks.whatHappened: The club kept winning for several years and the deal was heavily criticised as a vanity purchase. Then its main owner's property empire collapsed. On 6 January 2025 the club, by then called Guangzhou FC, disbanded because it could not clear its debts.
blocks.lesson: A deal done on a good mood is still a deal. Know who else is on the shareholder list, because their collapse becomes your problem.

blocks.text: Fifteen-minute call. $192 million. Don't try this at home.

blocks.name: The buying spree: UCWeb, Youku, Lazada, SCMP, Ele.me
blocks.idea: Buy into whatever would keep Chinese users inside Alibaba's world, and reach overseas: a mobile browser, a YouTube-like video site, a Southeast Asian store, an English newspaper and a food delivery app.
blocks.decision: Phones were changing how people shopped, and by 2014 Joe Tsai had driven more than $3.8 billion of deals across mapping, education and more. The newspaper purchase raised press-freedom worries, and Alibaba promised to be objective and fair.
blocks.howStarted: Stakes first, then control. UCWeb came through investments in 2009 and 2013 and full ownership in 2014. Youku began with a 16.5% stake.
blocks.funding: Alibaba's cash and shares. UCWeb cost about $2 billion. Youku cost about $5 billion in all. Lazada took $1 billion in 2016. SCMP cost $266 million. The Ele.me deal in 2018 valued it at $9.5 billion.
blocks.whatHappened: The results are mixed. These deals gave Alibaba reach in phones, video and delivery, but they cost a great deal. Its 2026 results still name quick-delivery spending as a main reason profit fell.
blocks.lesson: Buying growth is easy when your share price is high. The hard question is what happens after the first press release.

blocks.name: Physical retail: Intime and Sun Art
blocks.idea: Mix online data with real department stores and giant supermarkets. Alibaba called this push New Retail.
blocks.decision: Alibaba paid up to test the theory at scale. It joined Intime's founder to take that chain private in a $2.6 billion deal in 2017, and spent $2.9 billion in 2017 and $3.6 billion in 2020 on Sun Art, which runs RT-Mart hypermarkets.
blocks.howStarted: As stakes in existing chains. Alibaba bought rather than built any stores.
blocks.funding: Alibaba's cash.
blocks.whatHappened: It reversed course as it refocused on its core business. In December 2024 it agreed to sell Intime for about 7.4 billion yuan and book a loss of about 9.3 billion yuan ($1.3 billion). About two weeks later it agreed to sell its Sun Art stake for about $1.6 billion, expecting a further 13.2 billion yuan loss.
blocks.lesson: A big idea with a catchy name can still lose billions. Decide in advance what result would prove you wrong.

blocks.name: MoneyGram bid (Ant Financial)
blocks.idea: Buy the American money-transfer company MoneyGram to give Alipay a global network overnight.
blocks.decision: It was the fast route to worldwide reach, and Ma had already met Donald Trump in 2017 to pitch his plans for America. But American scrutiny of Chinese investment was rising.
blocks.howStarted: A takeover bid worth $1.2 billion, led by Ant Financial.
blocks.funding: Ant offered $1.2 billion. The deal never closed, so the money was not paid to shareholders.
blocks.whatHappened: In January 2018 the deal was dropped after the US government's foreign investment review committee, CFIUS, refused to approve it.
blocks.lesson: In finance and data, governments can veto you. Find out who holds that veto before you announce anything.

blocks.name: Hupan University
blocks.idea: An elite school for founders already running real companies, named after the apartment estate where Alibaba began. Ma was its president and said it should last 300 years.
blocks.decision: Ma and eight other business leaders and academics, including Lenovo's Liu Chuanzhi, wanted to teach entrepreneurs to build lasting companies. He said he would accept unprofitable years and even graduates who competed with Alibaba.
blocks.howStarted: Founded in March 2015 in Hangzhou. Applicants needed at least three years in business, over 30 million yuan in revenue and three referees.
blocks.funding: Backing from Alibaba, according to Caixin, plus tuition of 580,000 yuan for the three-year course.
blocks.whatHappened: Ma said that in five years 11,788 people applied and 254 got in, about 2%. New enrolment stopped after Ant's IPO was halted. In May 2021, as new rules barred unapproved use of the word university, it renamed itself the Zhejiang Hupan Entrepreneurship Research Center. It said it had never been a degree-granting school.
blocks.lesson: Be careful what you put your name on. Prestige built on one person's reputation falls fast when that person loses favour.

blocks.name: Founders' charitable trusts and the Jack Ma Foundation
blocks.idea: Use a slice of Alibaba itself to pay for work on the environment, medicine, education and culture.
blocks.decision: Ma said he and his wife had long planned to earn money before 50 and give after it. The trusts were announced five months before the IPO. Fortune pointed out that the options came from the company and so diluted all shareholders, which made the gift a matter of debate.
blocks.howStarted: Announced in April 2014, based on an option grant approved by Alibaba's board in 2013.
blocks.funding: Options on 50 million Alibaba shares, about 2% of the company, at a $25 strike price. Fortune valued that at $3.4 billion at the IPO's top price.
blocks.whatHappened: Ma's giving now runs partly through the Jack Ma Foundation, which also handles media questions about him. When he retired from Alibaba, philanthropy and education were his stated focus.
blocks.lesson: Giving is easiest to set up before the big payday, when the shares are still cheap.

blocks.name: Ma's Kitchen, sea farming and a Bordeaux chateau
blocks.idea: Ma's personal interests after retiring: agriculture, sea farming, food and wine. He has said he is studying how to grow grass, tea and grapes and how to raise fish and cattle.
blocks.decision: In 2019 he said a new company might be in farming. He then visited farms and research institutes in China, Spain, the Netherlands and Japan. In 2023 he became a visiting professor at the University of Tokyo, where his research covers sustainable farming and food production.
blocks.howStarted: Château de Sours in Bordeaux came first, in 2016. A marine-themed investment company in Hainan followed in 2020. Hangzhou Ma's Kitchen Food was registered on 22 November 2023.
blocks.funding: His own money. Ma's Kitchen has registered capital of 10 million yuan, through a company 99.9% owned by him. The Hainan firm had 200 million yuan of registered capital, under a parent in which he holds 50%. The chateau's price was not disclosed.
blocks.whatHappened: Early reports said Ma's Kitchen would sell pre-packaged meals, since that is in its registered business scope. A former assistant denied this and said even he did not know what it would do. So far, little else has been published. Treat this one as an open question.
blocks.lesson: Registered capital and a business licence tell you a person's interest, not their success. Check back in five years before you call something a venture.

blocks.text: Count them. About a third of these flopped or got folded in.

Add it up and a pattern appears. His big wins, Alibaba.com, Taobao, Alipay and the cloud, all solved a problem he could see on the ground and were owned by his own team. His big losses were usually bought in a hurry, like the football club, the film company or the supermarkets, or were forced on customers, like Laiwang. __The lesson for you: be slow to buy and fast to test.__

The funding story starts with one awkward sentence from Ma to Joe Tsai. When Tsai said he wanted to join, Ma had to admit he could only pay $50 a month. Tsai had a comfortable job in private equity in Hong Kong, and Ma had not even formally set up his company. Tsai later recalled Ma admitting he knew nothing about finance or law and needing someone who could draw up the founders' agreement and raise capital.

That mattered more than it sounds. Ma had just been burned in Beijing by a stake that was promised but never pinned down. This time there would be a proper agreement among all 18 founders before any investor showed up. Tsai handled the paperwork and served as chief financial officer until 2013, negotiating with investors like Yahoo and SoftBank. __The most valuable early hire is often the person who is strong where you are weak.__
Very important for first-time founders! Get the agreement done early.
The first real money

In October 1999 Goldman Sachs led Alibaba's first round of venture capital. Venture capital means investors buy part of a young company, hoping it becomes huge. The round was ==$5 million==. Goldman put in $3.3 million, with money also coming from Fidelity, Investor AB, TDF and Transpac. Alibaba was still working out of a flat.

For example, here is how close Goldman Sachs came to one of the best trades in history. It sold its entire stake by early 2004 for $22 million, nearly seven times what it paid, which looked like a terrific result. Then the people who bought those shares made as much as 30 times their money by the time of the 2014 IPO.

The next round came fast. In January 2000 SoftBank, the Japanese group run by Masayoshi Son, led a ==$20 million== round. Ma told The Wall Street Journal that he and Son never discussed revenue or even a business model, only a shared vision. Both of them liked making quick decisions.
No revenue talk. $20 million. That was 2000. Don't expect this.

blocks.text: By summer 2000 the mood was close to a rock concert. Forbes described Ma on stage at midnight at a lakeside resort, telling 110 mostly young staff they would build one of the world's top ten websites. Behind the speech, the numbers were thin. Alibaba had nearly 200,000 members, most in China, but revenue might only hit $1 million that year and its losses would be many times bigger. Tsai estimated the remaining money would last about 18 months.

Then the bubble burst. American internet stocks had been falling since spring 2000, and by the end of that year Chinese websites were closing. Ma had spent the money on offices across the world. By the start of 2001 Alibaba had about $10 million left and was burning about $2 million every month. No investor would write another cheque. __Five months of life, and no way yet to make money.__
The old-economy man

In January 2001 Alibaba hired Savio Kwan, a veteran of 17 years at General Electric. A headhunter told him Ma did not need more website builders. He needed someone who could build a real company. Kwan soon sat down with Ma and Tsai and agreed on a plan they called the three B2Cs: back to China, back to the coast, back to the centre.

Kwan asked Ma for one strange favour. For 30 days, please don't answer calls from staff, because everyone is going to beg you to save them. Ma agreed and kept to it. It sounds cold, but it let the cuts happen fast. Meanwhile Ma, Tsai and other top leaders cut their own pay in half, according to a Chinese account of the crisis.

Then came the hard part. Kwan and Tsai flew out over Lunar New Year 2001 to deliver the news in person. Before he left, Kwan's wife asked if she should pack him a bulletproof vest, half as a joke, since a laid-off man elsewhere had recently killed colleagues. In the US they met all 40 staff, paid every contract in full, and offered anyone the choice of shares instead of cash. Only one or two took the shares, and those people later became very well off.
They offered stock. Almost everyone took cash. Read that again.

For example, Hong Kong's staff of 30 were told at a Lunar New Year dinner that only 8 could stay. One employee home in Shanghai for the holiday got the news by phone. In South Korea every employee was let go with three months' pay. Back in China, offices outside the coast were closed. Total staff fell from about 360 to 150.

In 30 days the burn fell from $2 million to ==$500,000 a month==, with $9 million still in the bank. That was 18 months of life, more than three times what they had before. Kwan later said the speed was the whole point, because a slower process would have cost another month's burn and much more misery. One deep cut, he believed, beats many small ones.
Finding the business model

Surviving was only half the job, because they still had no way to make real money. In a long debate, Ma, Tsai and Kwan asked whether they would pay bribes to win business from corporate buyers, and they decided they would not. That shut down several possible lines of revenue. It also pushed them towards the one customer who would not need bribing: the owner of a small exporting factory, who spends his own money.

So they sold to owners. Sales teams knocked on doors, and they taught factory bosses how to use the internet, sometimes training their staff too. Exporters paid to be listed and found by foreign buyers. __Ma later said this one product saved Alibaba.__ Kwan says it grew into a billion-dollar line of business that paid for Taobao and Alipay. Ma has said that by the end of 2002 the company made one dollar in profit.
One dollar of profit. Sometimes that's the milestone that matters.

Kwan also pushed something that looks soft but was not. Over seven hours, the leaders hammered Ma's beliefs down to nine written values. Half of every employee's rating was then tied to how they behaved against those values, and the other half to their results. New hires were trained for two to four weeks rather than a few hours. That culture work paid off in 2003, when SARS sent the entire company home and it kept running.

eBay had not come for Alibaba. It wanted Chinese consumers, and in 2002 it bought a third of EachNet, China's largest e-commerce company, founded by a Harvard graduate. In June 2003 it bought the rest. Its CEO Meg Whitman told the Wall Street Journal the competition amounted to small rivals nipping at its heels. eBay named China its second priority market after the United States, and it had far more money than Alibaba.

Ma looked at that and saw a threat three moves away. In America eBay earned plenty from small businesses. In China, where one person often runs the whole firm, the line between a shop owner and a shopper was blurry. If eBay grew, its power sellers would eventually overlap with Alibaba's customers. __So Ma built a consumer site not because consumers were his dream, but to protect his B2B business.__
Taobao began as defence. Most people assume it was the plan.

In 2003 a small team worked in secret in Ma's old apartment, just as SARS was closing down offices in China. Porter Erisman, an American executive at Alibaba, remembers visiting and finding people asleep on the floor, waiting for a blackout to end. Harvard's Felix Oberholzer-Gee points out that this was a lockdown project, built by engineers who had nowhere else to go.

Taobao launched in May 2003, and eBay's share at that moment was reported between 70% and 85%. The usual advice would be to give up or find a niche. Ma instead framed the fight in his own way, telling people eBay might be a shark in the ocean but he was a crocodile in the Yangtze. The point was to fight in home water.
How the underdog fought

First, price. eBay charged sellers to list items. Taobao promised free listing for three years, and then kept extending it. EBay called this unsustainable, but eBay was thinking like a company that needed Taobao's fees. Alibaba had a separate business paying its bills, and it had SoftBank, which had already beaten eBay in Japan through Yahoo Japan.

Second, advertising. eBay signed exclusive deals that kept Taobao off China's main portals. That hurt: by early 2004 Taobao's own managers were reporting that they could hardly spend the marketing budget. They went around the block by advertising on a large number of online bulletin boards. eBay had the large stage. Taobao went where internet users were already talking to each other.

Third, trust, and this was the decisive move. As Oberholzer-Gee tells it, Alibaba went after people who were too nervous to buy online at all, rather than fighting to steal eBay's existing users. It organised Taobao like a Chinese department store, so it felt familiar. Most importantly, it added Alipay, which held the buyer's money until the goods arrived. __You don't always have to beat your rival's customers. You can win the people your rival ignored.__

For example, imagine you are a Chinese student in 2004 with a bank card and no credit card, buying a phone from a stranger in another city. On EachNet many deals had happened offline, in the same town. On Taobao you pay Alipay, the seller ships, and your money only moves when you click to say it arrived. That one step removed your biggest fear.
They sold safety, not software. Think about what your customer fears.

Fourth, design for local habits. Global giants tend to run one system worldwide, and eBay moved its Chinese site onto its global platform, with fees and rules set for other countries. Business Insider's account, based on the documentary Crocodile in the Yangtze, says Taobao made its site busy and friendly while eBay removed features local users enjoyed. Taobao also had its own messaging tool, later merged under the name Ali Wangwang.

The numbers turned quickly. At the end of 2004 iResearch had eBay at 39% and Taobao at 37%, less than two years after launch. eBay drained its advertising budget but never found an answer to free. In December 2006 eBay confirmed it would become the minority partner in a joint venture with TOM Online, and China Economic Review called it a capitulation. By 2008 Taobao held over 80% of the market.

blocks.text: The problem with winning for free

Winning left one question open: how does a free site make money? Taobao's first attempt was to auction top search spots, in a twist where sellers paid only if a shopper actually bought. There was a huge backlash, as there usually is when you start charging. But when the team looked at the data, about 40% of users actually liked the idea, because they believed higher-paying sellers meant better goods. This insight led directly to Tmall.
When users complain, still read the data. Forty percent said yes.

blocks.text: Ma first met Jerry Yang around 1998, while working in Beijing. Walks together on the Great Wall became a friendship, and the friendship became a negotiation that finished at the Pebble Beach resort in California. On 11 August 2005 Yahoo agreed to swap ==$1 billion== in cash and its China business for about 40% of Alibaba. That is a huge sum for a company that had made its first dollar of profit less than three years before.

Why give up so much? Because eBay was still a giant and the war was expensive. Ma could now outspend almost anyone in China. Remember the China Pages lesson, though: this time he made sure the founders kept running the company. Reuters later summed up what Wall Street believed, which was that Yahoo had little real control over Alibaba despite its large stake. __He sold a big share without selling the steering wheel.__
He learned from China Pages. Money yes. Control no.
A first listing, a nasty fall

In November 2007 Alibaba.com listed in Hong Kong. An IPO, or initial public offering, is when a company first sells its shares to the public on a stock market. It raised nearly ==$1.5 billion== at HK$13.50 a share. On the first day the price nearly tripled, closing at HK$39.50 and valuing the business at about $25.6 billion. The sale drew record demand from Hong Kong's retail investors.

Then it fell, and kept falling. By early 2012 the shares were at HK$9.25, far below the price at which ordinary investors had bought in. Alibaba Group then offered to buy everyone out at exactly HK$13.50, the original price, in a deal worth about $2.5 billion. People who bought at the IPO broke even. People who bought at the first day's close lost about two-thirds of their money. A scheme document also shows paying members had dropped by 5.4% in 2011.

For example, suppose you bought 1,000 shares at the first-day close in 2007 for HK$39,500. In 2012 Alibaba paid you HK$13,500 for those same shares. A great company and a great day to buy are two different things.
The fraud inside the company

In February 2011 a scandal hit Alibaba.com. An internal investigation led by Savio Kwan found that ==2,326== Gold Supplier accounts had been used to cheat overseas buyers in 2009 and 2010, mostly by advertising cheap electronics with low minimum orders. The average claim was under $1,200. The company had paid out $1.7 million. About 100 of its 5,000 salespeople, plus some managers, had helped the fraudsters get past verification, either on purpose or through carelessness.

The chief executive David Wei and chief operating officer Elvis Lee resigned. The investigation said neither man had taken part in the fraud. But the board accepted that they should take responsibility for a breakdown in the company's culture, and Ma publicly said so too. __Ma sacrificed two senior people rather than let sales targets corrupt the brand.__
Sales targets without values will eventually eat your company.
The Alipay fight

The same year brought the fiercest argument of Ma's career. In June 2010 China's central bank issued rules requiring payment companies to get a licence, with clear guidance only for firms wholly owned by Chinese nationals. Alibaba was largely foreign-owned, by Yahoo and SoftBank. By early 2011 it had moved Alipay into a company owned by Chinese nationals and majority owned by Ma. Alipay got its licence that May.

Yahoo said this happened without its knowledge, and the row went public. Critics said Ma had moved one of the group's most valuable assets into his own hands. Ma's side argued that the licence rules left no other way to keep Alipay alive. In July 2011 they settled. Alibaba would get ==37.5%== of Alipay's value at a future sale or IPO, but with a floor of $2 billion and a cap of $6 billion, plus a share of about half of Alipay's pre-tax profit until then. Analysts told Reuters Yahoo had got the short end.
A founder moved a key asset. Was it right? You decide.

The structure also shows something most people miss about how Chinese internet companies are owned. China limits foreign ownership in many online businesses. So Alibaba, like its peers, used a VIE, or variable interest entity: local companies hold the licences, while the foreign-listed company gets the profits through contracts. In Alibaba's case the most important of those local companies were majority owned by Ma personally, and minority owned by Simon Xie. Investors bought shares under that arrangement knowing the contracts might not work as well as direct ownership.
Merchants against Ma

That October, Taobao Mall said it would raise the annual fee for merchants from 6,000 yuan to between 30,000 and 60,000 yuan, along with bigger deposits. Small sellers revolted online. Thousands bought goods from big stores and immediately demanded refunds, which pulled those stores down in the rankings. Around 40,000 people gathered in one online chatroom to plan more. By December protesters in Hong Kong had put up a funeral effigy of Ma near Times Square.

Alibaba said it had good reason to think counterfeiters were among those organising the protest, and it did not cancel its plan. The higher fees were pushed back to the following October. This was a preview of a harder truth: the platform that gave small sellers their start would one day be the landlord they resented.
Buying back the company

In September 2012 Alibaba bought back half of Yahoo's holding for about ==$7.6 billion==. That included 523 million shares for $7.08 billion, paid mostly in cash with the rest in preferred shares, plus $550 million to change the licence deal with Yahoo. So Yahoo had made back several times its original investment, and still owned 23%. It would sell more at the IPO, and TIME estimated it could take in as much as $8.3 billion before tax in that sale alone.

Look at the ownership numbers in the Hong Kong filing from April 2012. Yahoo held 41.7%, SoftBank 31.8% and Ma just ==7.3%==. Most people think a founder of his fame must own the majority. By then he was a small minority shareholder in his own company, leading it with trust, voting agreements and later a special partnership structure.
7.3% of the company. Yet he ran it. Study how.
The record IPO

Alibaba wanted to list in Hong Kong, but the exchange would not accept its plan. The company's partnership, then 30 senior managers, would have the exclusive right to nominate a majority of the board, regardless of how few shares they held. Hong Kong's regulators would not accept giving partners that power regardless of shareholding. Alibaba took the listing to New York instead. In July 2010 the group had formally named this body Lakeside Partners, after the estate where Ma's apartment stood.

On 18 September 2014 the shares were priced at ==$68== each. They opened the next day at $92.70 and rose 38% by the close. With extra shares sold to meet demand, the deal hit ==$25 billion==, beating the previous global record of $22.1 billion set by Agricultural Bank of China. That first day valued Alibaba at nearly $230 billion, more than Amazon and eBay put together.

Ma sold too. He was set to sell at least 12.75 million shares, which at the $68 price is about $867 million, with up to 2.7 million more if the extra allotment was used. Forbes valued the rest of his stake at the time at nearly $10 billion. And the $20 million from SoftBank in 2000 was now worth perhaps $50 billion or more, one of the greatest venture returns ever made.

blocks.text: The first public warning shot came just four months after the IPO. In January 2015 China's business regulator published a harsh report saying Alibaba had not done enough to stop fake goods on its sites. It emerged that the report had been written in July and held back so as not to disturb the New York listing. Alibaba hit back and accused a named official of bias, which AP called almost unheard of in China. The dispute rattled investors and the share price tumbled.

Ma was by now behaving almost like a statesman. Days before Donald Trump's inauguration, in January 2017, Ma visited Trump Tower and spoke of helping create a million American jobs by letting small US businesses sell to China. In September 2018, as tariffs grew, he told China's state news agency that the conditions for that promise no longer existed. Economists had always been doubtful about the math, because it was never clear how selling to Asia would translate into jobs.

That same month he announced his retirement. He had already given up the CEO title in 2013, and Daniel Zhang had held it since 2015. On 10 September 2019, his 55th birthday, he stepped down as executive chairman. Reuters said it was very rare for a founder of such a company to leave so early. He still held 6.22% and a seat in the partnership. Two months later Alibaba raised up to ==$12.9 billion== in a second listing in Hong Kong, the city that had turned down its structure before the 2014 IPO.
He retired at 55. The biggest crisis came after.
The largest IPO that never happened

In 2020 Ant was ready to list in both Shanghai and Hong Kong. Through a chain of holding partnerships, Ma controlled 50.52% of Ant, even though his actual economic share was far smaller. He owned 34% of a small company called Hangzhou Yunbo, and a separate agreement among its four owners gave him final say. Alibaba itself owned about a third. Ant's revenue was growing at 43% in the first nine months of 2020.

The deal was gigantic. Ant priced it to raise at least ==$34.5 billion==, valuing the company at about $315 billion. Retail investors in Shanghai and Hong Kong placed orders worth over ==$3 trillion==. Institutional investors in Shanghai asked for more than 284 times what was on offer. Ma's fortune climbed by billions on paper, and he was China's richest person.

On 24 October 2020, days before the listing, Ma spoke at the Bund Finance Summit in Shanghai with senior regulators in the audience. He said China's banks had a pawnshop mindset, always asking for collateral. He said good innovation should fear outdated regulation, not regulation itself, and that you cannot run an airport with the rules of a train station. He compared the global Basel banking rules to a club for old people. It was a remarkably public attack, at a very sensitive moment, on the people who decide what Ant is allowed to do.

Events then moved within days. On 2 November he and Ant's executives were summoned to a rare joint meeting with the central bank and three other financial regulators, and the same day draft rules on online lending came out. On 3 November the Shanghai exchange suspended the listing, citing changes in the regulatory environment. Hong Kong followed. Trading had been due to start on 5 November. Reuters reported, citing unnamed officials and executives, that the speech set off the chain of events. Ant's lending model had also been a growing concern for regulators.
Two days from the record. Then nothing. Think about timing.

The cost grew from there. In December 2020 a central bank official told Ant to return to its roots as a payments provider and fix what he called illegal credit, insurance and wealth management activities. In April 2021 Alibaba paid a record antitrust fine of 18.2 billion yuan, about ==$2.8 billion==. Antitrust means rules against abusing a dominant market position. Regulators found Alibaba had abused its dominant position over rivals and merchants, and exclusivity was at the heart of the debate. CEO Daniel Zhang said the fine would have no material negative impact.

Ma largely vanished from public view and was later seen abroad, including in Europe and Asia. Forbes says he spent about a year overseas before returning to China in 2023, when he visited a school in Hangzhou. Hupan stopped enrolling students. In January 2023 Ant announced that Ma would give up control, with ten people now voting independently. Ma's share of Ant's voting rights fell from over 50% to about ==6.2%==. Neither Alibaba nor any other shareholder would control it.

In July 2023 regulators fined Ant and its units 7.12 billion yuan, or ==$984 million==, for failures in governance, consumer protection, payments and anti-money-laundering. Ant said it had completed its required changes and would comply. A day later it offered to buy back up to 7.6% of its shares from investors at a price valuing the company at ==$78.54 billion==. A share buyback is when a company purchases its own stock. That price was 75% below the IPO valuation. By Bloomberg's count the clash had cost Alibaba and Ant over $1.14 trillion in lost value.

__Here is the fairest way to read this.__ Ma's speech wasn't the only reason. Ant's lending had grown far ahead of the rules, and new regulations for lenders and financial groups were already coming. But Ma had built Alipay by moving ahead of the rules, once telling staff he would go to jail for it if he had to, and for years he was allowed to. In 2020 that stopped within a single week.
Know whose permission your whole business depends on.
The rivals who didn't wait

While Alibaba was distracted, a younger company was eating its lunch. PDD Holdings, which runs Pinduoduo and Temu, sold cheap goods to shoppers looking for bargains. In the third quarter of 2023 PDD's revenue grew 94% while Alibaba's grew 9%. In late November its market value reached about $185 billion against Alibaba's $195 billion, and one day it briefly passed Alibaba's. Market value means the price of one share times all the shares.

An employee posted on Alibaba's internal forum about being unable to sleep over the news. Then the founder, who had stayed mostly silent for three years, replied. Ma congratulated PDD on its decisions and execution, and told staff he was convinced Alibaba would change and return to its founding mission. __Praising your rival to your own staff takes confidence, and the message was that Alibaba was the challenger again.__
He praised the rival, in writing, to his own people.

The plan for Alibaba kept shifting. In March 2023 it announced its biggest shake-up ever: six separate units, most of them able to list on their own. Its US shares had lost nearly 70% since the crackdown began. By November it had cancelled the cloud spin-off and blamed American chip export limits, and $20 billion of value disappeared in a day. In March 2024 it dropped the Cainiao IPO. In June 2023 long-time lieutenants Joe Tsai and Eddie Wu took over as chairman and CEO. Then it sold its supermarkets and department stores, and refocused on shopping and cloud.

Ma's own trades in those months are revealing. In November 2023 his family trusts disclosed plans to sell 10 million US-traded shares worth about $871 million. The stock dropped, and the plan, reportedly meant to fund his new initiatives, was held off. By January 2024 it emerged he had instead bought $50 million of shares in Hong Kong. Soon afterwards SoftBank finished selling down, booking a final gain of $8.5 billion, about 425 times its original outlay of $20 million. That left Ma and Tsai as the company's largest holders.

For example, look at how SoftBank shrank its Alibaba position. Alibaba made up 48% of SoftBank's assets in 2020. By May 2024 its finance chief described that share as almost zero, with most of its value now tied to chip designer Arm. The most famous early bet in Asian tech was gone in four years.

By February 2025 the mood had shifted. Ma was seated at a symposium with President Xi Jinping alongside the heads of BYD, Tencent, Xiaomi and Huawei, where Xi told private companies they had broad prospects. Analysts read this as a sign that the crackdown was fading. Alibaba had also turned hard towards AI, with its Qwen models and own chips, and a cloud business growing fast again. In August 2026 it sold HK$80 billion of new shares at a discount to pay for this, and Yicai reported, citing a source, that Ma put in more than HK$600 million of his own money to buy shares.

The spending shows up in the accounts. Revenue for the year to March 2026 was RMB1.02 trillion ($148.4 billion). But in the June 2026 quarter net income fell 75%, as capital spending rose 75% to RMB67.7 billion. Cloud revenue grew 45%. __Alibaba is making a bet in AI that feels just like the 2009 cloud bet: years of spending while critics ask whether it will pay.__ Whether it does is unknown as we write.
Where the money actually is

So what is he actually worth? It depends on who you ask. As of 2 November 2026, Forbes put him at ==$25.1 billion==, number 98 in the world. As of 1 November, Bloomberg's index put him at ==$40.8 billion==, number 50. A gap of $15.7 billion on one person sounds absurd, but it is honest. Nobody outside can see his bank account, and Bloomberg's estimate adds a large pile of cash.

Bloomberg's breakdown holds one of the biggest surprises in this book. It values his Alibaba shares, about 4% of the company, at $9.33 billion, and his Ant stake at $5.14 billion. It also lists a small holding in Huayi Brothers, the film company, at under $10 million. Those add up to about $14.5 billion. __So roughly $26 billion of Bloomberg's total, nearly two-thirds, is simply estimated cash from dividends and share sales.__ The man most identified with Alibaba holds, by that estimate, far more money outside it.

blocks.text: His peak was about ==$61.7 billion==, just before the Ant crisis. That means his fortune, on one estimate or the other, is 35% to 60% smaller than it was six years ago. His direct share of Alibaba has also kept falling: 7.3% in 2012, 6.22% in 2019, 4.8% by mid-2020 and about 4% now. Part of that came from selling, and part from giving shares to charity.

factCheck.method: Primary documents were preferred where available: Alibaba's 2014 prospectus and 2015 annual report (SEC), Alibaba.com's 2011 and 2012 Hong Kong exchange filings, Ant's 2020 prospectus, Yahoo's 2011 SEC note, Alibaba's 2026 results, and first-person accounts from Ma (Inc., 2008) and Savio Kwan (2020). Established press filled the gaps. Chinese-language state and business press supplied the pre-1999 detail. Bloomberg, Reuters, AP, NYT, Guardian and BBC pages refused direct automated reading in this run, so those sources are cited only for what search highlights displayed, and we did not route around the refusals. Direct quotation was deliberately kept to one short line, with everything else restated in our own words. Net worth figures are dated estimates and were the latest published when checked on 3 November 2026.

disputed.note: Guangming Daily and CNTV say 1992. People's Daily Online and China Securities Journal say 1994. China Economic Net says 1991. We used 1992 because the Guangming account is the most detailed and fits Ma's own statement to Inc. that the climate improved in 1992.

Guangming: 3,000 yuan of capital, 1,500 yuan monthly rent, first month under 1,000 yuan. People's Daily Online and China Economic Net: first month's income 700 yuan against rent of 2,000 yuan. We gave a range.

Ma (Inc.) and Forbes say about $2,000. Jiemian says about 20,000 yuan. China Securities Journal says 7,000 yuan. A Baidu Baike entry says 100,000 yuan, but Baike was not treated as reliable. We used $2,000.

disputed.claim: China Telecom's price for China Pages
disputed.note: Ma told Inc. $185,000 for a joint venture with five board seats to his two. Forbes in 2000 said the equivalent of $240,000 for a 70% stake. Other accounts name Hangzhou Telecom as the state partner. Both figures are given.

disputed.claim: Size of the team Ma took to Beijing
disputed.note: China Securities Journal implies 6 people in total. Jiemian lists 12 names. We said 5 to 12.
Forbes says the site launched in March 1999. The prospectus gives 28 June 1999 for the holding company. Baike-style sources give 10 March. Both of the better-sourced dates are shown.

A widely repeated story says Son offered $40 million within minutes and Ma accepted only $20 million. WSJ (2000) and the prospectus confirm the $20 million round, led by SoftBank, but we found no strong source for the offer itself, so it is left out.
Savio Kwan says about $10 million. A China.com account says $7 million. We used Kwan, who was there.

disputed.claim: eBay's China share when Taobao launched
disputed.note: Stanford GSB says over 70%. AP says 80% for EachNet. HBR and Business Insider say 85%. Measurement dates differ. We said over 70%, and 70% to 85% in the narrative.
HBR's podcast says Ma's apartment in Shanghai. Chinese timelines and Alibaba's own history say Hangzhou. We wrote his old apartment; the Hangzhou version is better supported.

The prospectus says $30 million of convertible notes in 2003 and a series totalling $50 million into the Taobao entity. Helen Wang's book says $56 million. Chinese reports refer to $60 million or an $82 million round in 2004. We used the prospectus.
The prospectus says about 40% fully diluted. Reuters in 2011 said 43%. The 2012 filing says 41.7%. Figures vary with timing and dilution.
AP and Bloomberg say at least $34.5 billion. Reuters says $37 billion, including the extra share option. Both are correct on different bases.

Caixin and Alibaba's annual report cite 8.8%. Bloomberg calculates 9.9% from the 2020 prospectus. Ma's voting share after January 2023 is about 6.2%, an FT calculation repeated by Al Jazeera and The Straits Times.

The exchange cited a changed regulatory environment and draft lending rules. Reuters reported, from anonymous officials and executives, that Ma's speech set off the chain of events. Reports that Xi Jinping personally ordered the halt could not be verified from a source we could read, so the book does not state this.

Forbes: $25.1 billion on 2 Nov 2026. Bloomberg: $40.8 billion on 1 Nov 2026. The gap comes largely from how much accumulated cash each assumes. The $26 billion cash figure is our subtraction from Bloomberg's listed asset values, not a number Bloomberg states.
Reported by Yicai from one unnamed source. Alibaba's filing named only Tsai and Wu. Treated as reported, not confirmed.
China Daily says HK$13.13 billion ($1.69 billion). Taipei Times and Mingtiandi say up to HK$12.3 billion ($1.6 billion). Different bases; we said about $1.6 billion.
Alibaba's filing disclosed a planned sale of about $871 million. SCMP and Asia Business Daily, citing The Paper, reported that it did not go ahead. We describe it as reportedly put on hold.
